title: After the Storm | 09/21/2026 Market Strategy
text: Asset Management 09/21/2026 Market Strategy John Stoltzfus September 21, 2026 Printable Version Share x, formerly known as Twitter linkedin share close After the Storm Stocks Bounce Between Gains and Losses - Could This Be the New Normal? Key Takeaways The Federal Reserve’s unanimous vote to hike rates last Wednesday altered the dynamics in US equity and bond markets as policy materials indicated that most Fed governors expect another rate hike by year-end. Renewed resilience in the labor market and consumer demand in the face of rising price pressures this summer flipped the balance of risks in the Fed’s outlook toward inflation control over bolstering the labor market. In our view, the Fed’s move could help moderate or reverse the rise in yields at the long end of the Treasury curve if markets see these moves as indications of the Fed’s vigilance on inflation control. Last Wednesday the 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.02%, it's highest since June of 2007. With oil prices topping $100/bbl and diesel fuel prices at record highs, markets await some signs of progress on a resolution to the conflagration in the Middle East. This week’s data calendar is sparse on major releases, with just new home sales, durable goods orders and a revision to the Michigan sentiment indicator due. With a relatively light calendar of economic data this week, traders and investors will likely be focused on news items tied to any developments emerging from the high level meetings between the US and China already underway stateside culminating in a tête-à-tête between President Trump and Chairman Xi of China on Friday. In our view, the number and magnitude of future Fed hikes matter much more than this first increase, which the central bank suggested might be followed by another later this year. Any progress reported from a week of meetings between the US and China that is tied to trade, the Strait of Hormuz, the global price of oil, and inflation could alter the direction the markets stateside and abroad take on a given day. With Q3 earnings season “not ready for prime time” until the big US banks begin reporting on October 13, any corporate developments and commentary of worth in the interim could gain attention and commentary from prognosticators and market participants moving the market. Last week saw markets wobble, stabilize, and then wobble some more as traders and investors pondered the effects of a quarter point hike by the Fed to its benchmark rate and gave consideration to a broad array of outcomes for the US economy, the world economy as well as the effect of the rate hike on the stock market, the bond market, corporate earnings, the consumer, and jobs growth. Depending on whom you spoke to or were listening to last week, commentary ranged from “dark shadows” to “the end of the world as we know it” to “what me worry?” to “everything’s gonna be alright. For now, we’ll be focused on the fundamentals and stay data dependent with eyes on the Fed, the economy, the behavior of the bond market along with corporate trends in revenue, earnings growth, and innovation. We’ll be giving less weight to reads given from consumer sentiment surveys and pay even more attention to consumer behavior--as well as the condition of the job market. Last Week’s Market Action Last week closed with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average marginally lower on the week, respectively off 1.7% and 0.8%. The NASDAQ Composite (weighted some 55% in technology companies) edged higher, adding 0.72% over the course of the week as the sector “caught a bid” from traders and investors. Mid-cap and small-cap stocks took the Fed’s adjustment to interest rates to heart slipping 1.71% and 2.04% respectively on the week with some of their price decline reflective of concern about the effect of higher interest rates on borrowing and refinancing costs. In our view, the number and magnitude of future Fed hikes matter much more than this first increase, which the central bank suggested might be followed by another later this year. We won’t jump to conclusions for now. What’s with Our S&P 500 Price Target? Last week several strategists and at least one economist adjusted their price targets lower for this year or for the next twelve months. Ironically many had just recently adjusted their price targets higher in the bull run that took the S&P 500 to its most recent record high of 7,798.99 on August 13. Back in August, some of our readers asked us if we were planning to raise our 2026 year-end target of 8,100 which we had initiated last December for the S&P 500. At the time we responded, “Not yet as the discipline we’ve established is not to raise our target until the market closes at or above our target.” That said, for now we will maintain our year-end target of 8100 for the S&P 500. We should note that our self-imposed target price discipline allows us to lower our target or even eliminate it should economic or market conditions appear to call for such an action. At this juncture with the S&P 500 closing at 7650.55--a little less than 6% away from our 8,100-target price and with the market up 11.8% year-to-date--we’ll continue to weigh the fundamentals as well as the real and perceived risks on the proverbial landscape while sticking for now with 8,100 by year-end. Stay tuned. Name: John Stoltzfus Title: Chief Investment Strategist, Oppenheimer Asset Management Inc.
